uzbek: biror narsadan uzoqroq yurmoq / chetlab o'tmoq
usage: Used when advising others to avoid popular tourist traps or unsafe areas.
common_mistakes: Steering clear to the crowds (wrong preposition)
Steer clear for the city center
example_sentences: We decided to steer clear of the main square during the festival as it was too crowded.
Local residents usually steer clear of that district after dark.
If you want an authentic meal, steer clear of the restaurants near the tourist information center.
I suggest we steer clear of the coastal road until the storm passes.
Most travelers steer clear of the city center during rush hour.
native_notes: More idiomatic than 'avoid'. It implies active effort to bypass something unpleasant or overwhelming.

uzbek: turistlar ko'p bormaydigan joy, gavjum bo'lmagan yo'l
usage: Used to describe remote or less explored destinations.
grammar_pattern: to go/travel + off the beaten track
example_sentences: We prefer finding quiet villages off the beaten track rather than staying in big hotels.
Exploring regions off the beaten track is the best way to understand the local culture.
It was a small cafe, well off the beaten track, but the food was incredible.
Traveling off the beaten track requires more planning and a good sense of direction.
The island is still relatively off the beaten track and remains unspoiled.
collocations: find spots off the beaten track
native_notes: Very common in travel writing. Sounds much more adventurous than just saying 'remote'.

usage: Describing locations that are very close to one another.
grammar_pattern: to be a stone's throw from + location
alternatives: A hop, skip, and a jump away
example_sentences: Our hotel was just a stone's throw from the beach.
The museum is a stone's throw from the central railway station.
Finding an apartment a stone's throw from the city center is quite expensive.
We were a stone's throw from the border, so the crossing was very fast.
Even though it's a bustling market, the quiet park is just a stone's throw away.
collocations: a stone's throw from the beach
a stone's throw from the city
perfectly located a stone's throw from
native_notes: Use this to emphasize convenience when describing accommodation or proximity to landmarks.

uzbek: muhitidan bahra olmoq, atmosferaga singib ketmoq
usage: Describing the act of relaxing and experiencing the vibe of a new place.
grammar_pattern: to soak up + noun (atmosphere, culture, vibes)
example_sentences: We spent the afternoon sitting in a sidewalk cafe just soaking up the atmosphere.
You need a few days in Rome to really soak up the atmosphere of the city.
It's worth visiting the night market just to soak up the atmosphere.
Instead of rushing through the sights, take time to soak up the atmosphere of the local neighborhood.
She sat by the harbor, soaking up the atmosphere of the bustling port.
native_notes: Perfect for Speaking Part 2 when describing a trip. It shows a deeper level of travel experience.
russian: наслаждаться окружающей средой, погружаться в атмосферу

usage: Used when talking about packing minimally to move around easily.
common_mistakes: Travel lightly (usually used as an adverb, not the idiom)
example_sentences: I always try to travel light so I don't have to wait for my luggage at the airport.
If you are planning to hike, you really need to travel light.
Traveling light makes it much easier to use public transport in foreign cities.
She learned the hard way to travel light after lugging a huge suitcase through Tokyo.
Experienced backpackers know that it's best to travel light.
collocations: travel light with just a backpack
opposites: pack everything including the kitchen sink
native_notes: A very common phrase for frequent travelers. It implies practicality and efficiency.

expression: to get off the beaten track
usage: Used when describing travel experiences that avoid crowded, touristy locations in favour of more authentic or remote areas.
grammar_pattern: to get off the beaten track + (prepositional phrase)
common_mistakes: saying 'get out of the beaten track'
using it to mean just 'getting lost'
example_sentences: I prefer to get off the beaten track when I visit a new country.
We decided to rent a car and get off the beaten track to see the real landscape.
It’s not always easy to get off the beaten track without a local guide.
Some travellers spend their whole trip trying to get off the beaten track.
If you want to get off the beaten track, avoid the city centre entirely.
collocations: thoroughly get off the beaten track
prefer to get off the beaten track
attempt to get off the beaten track
manage to get off the beaten track
a chance to get off the beaten track
opposites: to stay on the main tourist trail
native_notes: Implies a sense of adventure and a desire for authenticity rather than just avoiding people.

uzbek: sayyohlar uchun mo'ljallangan qimmat va sun'iy joy
usage: Used to describe a place that attracts many tourists but is considered overpriced or lacking in genuine quality.
common_mistakes: calling a popular museum a tourist trap just because it is busy
using 'tourist trap' for an entire city
example_sentences: Don't eat at that restaurant; it's a total tourist trap.
I avoid the main square because it's nothing but a tourist trap.
The gift shop was clearly a tourist trap with inflated prices.
We managed to avoid most of the tourist traps during our stay in Venice.
Is this museum actually worth the money or is it just a tourist trap?
native_notes: Very negative connotation; implies the business is specifically exploiting tourists for profit.
russian: дорогое и искусственное место для туристов

uzbek: juda kam mablag' bilan sayohat qilmoq
usage: Used when describing someone who travels while spending very little money.
common_mistakes: using it to mean travelling quickly
alternatives: to keep costs to a minimum
example_sentences: When I was a student, I used to travel on a shoestring.
It is possible to travel on a shoestring if you stay in hostels.
We are planning to travel on a shoestring through Southeast Asia this summer.
Travelling on a shoestring is a great way to meet fellow adventurers.
You don't need a huge budget if you're prepared to travel on a shoestring.
collocations: manage to travel on a shoestring
decide to travel on a shoestring
the experience of travelling on a shoestring
prefer to travel on a shoestring
native_notes: Suggests resourcefulness and prioritizing experiences over material comfort.

expression: to be a home away from home
uzbek: o'z uyingdagidek qulay va iliq maskan
usage: Used to describe a place (hotel, town, or café) where one feels as comfortable and relaxed as one does in their own home.
grammar_pattern: place + is/to be + a home away from home
example_sentences: This little guesthouse has become my home away from home whenever I visit London.
We want our hotel to be a home away from home for all our guests.
That small library is a real home away from home for me.
After months on the road, that villa felt like a home away from home.
They treated us so well that the place truly felt like a home away from home.
collocations: truly a home away from home
feel like a home away from home
act as a home away from home
be considered a home away from home
become a home away from home
native_notes: Conveys warmth, safety, and personal belonging.
russian: уютное и теплое место, как ваш собственный дом

uzbek: juda kam pul bilan, iqtisod qilib
usage: Used to explain that someone is traveling with very little money and must be careful with spending.
grammar_pattern: to travel + on a shoestring budget
example_sentences: Back when I was a student, I traveled through Europe on a shoestring budget.
It’s surprisingly easy to visit Asia on a shoestring budget if you stay in hostels.
They managed to have a great holiday even on a shoestring budget.
Traveling on a shoestring budget forced us to be more creative with our plans.
You don't need a fortune to see the world; I’m doing it on a shoestring budget.
native_notes: A 'shoestring' is a thin lace; the metaphor suggests that the resources are stretched as thin as possible.

usage: Used when referring to a short stop during a longer journey to eat, refuel, or rest.
example_sentences: We decided to make a pit stop in a small town to grab some lunch.
The drive is long, so we’ll definitely need a few pit stops.
Let’s make a quick pit stop at the petrol station before we hit the motorway.
The museum was a great pit stop during our walk across the city.
He stopped for a coffee, which ended up being a two-hour pit stop.
native_notes: Originating from Formula 1 racing, it is now commonly used for any short interruption in a trip, usually implying a quick departure.

usage: Used to describe a very short trip to a place, often when you have very little time.
common_mistakes: a fast visit (flying visit is the idiomatic phrase)
a quick trip (correct but flying visit is higher level)
example_sentences: It was just a flying visit; I was only in London for six hours.
I can only pay a flying visit to your city, but I hope to see the main sights.
She made a flying visit to see her parents before catching her flight.
The CEO’s flying visit to the branch office lasted less than a day.
Due to my tight schedule, it will have to be a flying visit this time.
native_notes: Use this to describe a trip where you feel rushed. It sounds much more natural than saying 'I stayed for a short time'.

usage: Used to describe a very short distance between two locations.
grammar_pattern: be a stone's throw from + location
example_sentences: Our hotel was a stone's throw from the beach, which was incredibly convenient.
The train station is just a stone's throw from the museum entrance.
It’s great living a stone's throw from the city center.
We found a lovely café that was a stone's throw from our hostel.
Even though it's a stone's throw from the main road, the area is surprisingly quiet.
collocations: a stone's throw from the coast
a stone's throw from the station
a stone's throw from the city
native_notes: This is a classic British idiom. It makes descriptive writing in IELTS Task 2 or Speaking much more vivid.

usage: Used when there are so many good options that it becomes difficult to choose.
grammar_pattern: to be spoilt for choice + regarding/of
alternatives: to have an abundance of options
example_sentences: When it comes to restaurants in London, you are truly spoilt for choice.
With so many excursions available, tourists are spoilt for choice.
We were spoilt for choice with all the different types of street food.
In the museum gift shop, I was spoilt for choice and bought too many souvenirs.
Travelers are spoilt for choice if they visit the region in the summer.
collocations: spoilt for choice when it comes to
native_notes: A very common British phrase. It sounds natural and advanced in both formal writing and casual conversation.

usage: Used to describe a place that is wonderful but not widely known or visited.
example_sentences: This small beach is a real hidden gem; you won't find it in most guidebooks.
The cafe is a hidden gem tucked away in a quiet side street.
I’m hesitant to share the location, as I want to keep this hidden gem to myself.
For a quiet weekend, this town is an absolute hidden gem.
We were surprised to find such a hidden gem in the middle of the busy city.
native_notes: Used when someone feels they have discovered something special that others have missed.
russian: красивое место, о котором мало кто знает

expression: to be off the beaten track
uzbek: mashhur bo'lmagan, kam odam boradigan joy
usage: Used to describe remote or less touristy travel destinations.
grammar_pattern: to be + off the beaten track
common_mistakes: off the beaten path (also correct but 'track' is very British)
example_sentences: We prefer staying in small villages that are off the beaten track.
He spent his summer holiday trekking in regions completely off the beaten track.
The best part of the trip was finding a local café off the beaten track.
Is there any place left in Europe that is truly off the beaten track?
If you go off the beaten track, you'll see a much more authentic side of the country.
collocations: find places off the beaten track
native_notes: Very common in travel writing to sound more adventurous and less 'touristy'.

usage: Describes cities that are full of energy, noise, and constant movement.
example_sentences: Tokyo is a bustling city that never seems to sleep.
Despite being a bustling city, it has many quiet parks to escape to.
I find it exhausting to stay in such a bustling city for too long.
The capital is a bustling city full of culture and history.
If you enjoy a bustling city, you will love the nightlife here.
native_notes: Often used positively to suggest excitement, but can imply being overwhelmed depending on context.

usage: Used when recommending a major landmark or attraction to someone.
common_mistakes: it is a must to see (awkward)
it is a see-must (wrong word order)
alternatives: it is a highlight of the city
example_sentences: If you visit Paris, the Louvre is an absolute must-see.
The view from the top of the tower is a must-see for all visitors.
Most people agree that the historical centre is a must-see.
I really think the night market is a must-see while you're here.
Whether you like history or not, the castle is a must-see.
native_notes: Functions as a noun here, which makes it very efficient and natural for recommendations.

uzbek: sayyohlardan pul undirish uchun mo'ljallangan qimmat joy
usage: Used to describe a place that is overpriced and designed only to attract tourists rather than locals.
common_mistakes: it is a trap for tourists
example_sentences: Don't eat at that restaurant; it's a total tourist trap.
The souvenir shop near the cathedral is a bit of a tourist trap.
I avoid the city center during summer as it feels like one big tourist trap.
We felt disappointed because the museum turned out to be a complete tourist trap.
Local people never go to that cafe, so you know it's a tourist trap.
native_notes: Used pejoratively; indicates that the quality of food or service is low and the price is high.
russian: дорогое место, предназначенное для вымогательства денег у туристов

usage: Often used in IELTS Speaking Part 3 or Writing Task 2 to explain the educational benefits of travel.
example_sentences: Studying abroad is an excellent way to broaden your horizons.
Traveling to different countries certainly helps to broaden your horizons.
I believe that meeting people from diverse backgrounds helps broaden one's horizons.
The primary benefit of a gap year is that it helps young people broaden their horizons.
Reading and traveling are the two best ways to broaden your horizons.
native_notes: Refers to both physical travel and mental growth; very high-scoring phrase for academic contexts.

expression: to be on a shoestring budget
uzbek: juda kam pul bilan (byudjetda) sayohat qilish
usage: Used when describing traveling with very little money.
grammar_pattern: to be on a shoestring budget
common_mistakes: to be on a string budget
example_sentences: We traveled across Europe on a shoestring budget as students.
It is possible to see the world even when you are on a shoestring budget.
Backpacking is great for those who are on a shoestring budget.
They lived on a shoestring budget while exploring Southeast Asia.
If you want to travel on a shoestring budget, you should stay in hostels.
native_notes: An idiom derived from the idea that a shoestring is very thin and limited; implies extreme financial caution.
russian: путешествие с очень небольшими деньгами (с ограниченным бюджетом).

usage: Standard phrase for sightseeing when visiting a new city or country.
example_sentences: We spent our first two days just seeing the sights in central London.
Are you going to see the sights while you're in Rome?
After we checked into the hotel, we grabbed a map and went to see the sights.
It’s impossible to see all the sights of Paris in just one weekend.
We hired a local guide to help us see the sights more efficiently.
collocations: best way to see the sights
native_notes: Slightly less formal than 'sightseeing', used very naturally in daily conversation.

usage: Used to describe the busy, noisy atmosphere of a city or a popular market.
grammar_pattern: the hustle and bustle of + noun
example_sentences: I love the hustle and bustle of Marrakech, especially the night market.
Sometimes you just need to escape the hustle and bustle of city life.
The train station was filled with the usual hustle and bustle of commuters.
We chose a quiet hotel to get away from the hustle and bustle of the tourist zone.
Despite the hustle and bustle, the city has a unique, charming rhythm.
native_notes: Very common collocation. Used as a fixed phrase; you don't use 'hustle' or 'bustle' separately in this context.
